catholic.theosis:
Catholic teaching includes the idea that God shares his own life with human beings, a doctrine often called divinization. The Catechism quotes the saying, found in early teachers such as Athanasius and later in Thomas Aquinas, that the Son of God became man so that we might become God, and it cites the Second Letter of Peter, that believers become partakers of the divine nature.

Catholics understand this as taking place through sanctifying grace, which unites a person to God and transforms him, and finally through the beatific vision, seeing God face to face. It does not mean that a human being becomes God in essence. The language is used less commonly in Catholic teaching than in Eastern Orthodoxy. A Protestant reader who speaks of union with Christ should note that Catholics use both, and that divinization is a way of describing what grace accomplishes.
lds.theosis:
Latter-day Saints teach that human beings are children of God who can become like him. The state which they describe as exaltation includes living in God's presence, becoming joint heirs with Christ, and receiving all that the Father has, and they speak of it as eternal progression.

Latter-day Saint teaching holds that human beings and God are of the same kind, though not equal, and that those who are exalted will continue to worship the Father and the Son. Church leaders have taught that God was once a man, but the church has not fully defined the details of that idea. The Eastern Orthodox teaching of theosis is similar in vocabulary but understands humans as sharing in God's life and not as becoming God. A Protestant reader should note that Latter-day Saints go further than most Christians in speaking of humans becoming like God.
oriental_ortho.theosis:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, including the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, teach theosis, or deification: that human beings are called to share, by grace, in the life of God, and to become partakers of the divine nature, as the Second Letter of Peter says. They draw on the teaching of early Fathers such as Athanasius of Alexandria, who said that God became man so that man might become god.

Theosis is understood as beginning in baptism and growing through the sacraments, prayer, fasting and love, and as finally completed in the age to come. It does not mean becoming God in essence. A Protestant reader who speaks of union with Christ should note that these churches use the language of deification to describe the goal of salvation, and that it is central to their monastic and liturgical traditions.
ortho.theosis:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches theosis, also called deification: that human beings are called to share in the life of God, and to become, by grace, what God is by nature. It draws on the Second Letter of Peter, which speaks of believers becoming partakers of the divine nature, and on the teaching of the Fathers, such as Athanasius, who said that God became man so that man might become god.

The Orthodox teach that this does not mean that a person becomes God in essence, but that he participates in God's uncreated energies, and is united with him. It begins in Baptism, grows through the sacraments, prayer and repentance, and is completed in the age to come. A Protestant reader will find that the Orthodox and many Protestants both speak of union with Christ, and should note that the Orthodox use the language of deification for it.
catholic.theotokos:
Catholics call Mary the Mother of God, in Greek Theotokos, meaning the one who bore God. The title was affirmed at the Council of Ephesus in 431, and it is used in Catholic teaching and prayer, for example in the Hail Mary, which asks Holy Mary, Mother of God, to pray for us.

The title is not intended to say that Mary is the source of God's divinity, but that the child she bore is the one person of the Son of God, who is God, and that she is therefore the mother of the person who is God. It was meant to protect the truth about Christ. A Protestant reader may hear the phrase as suggesting that Mary is greater than God. It is more accurate to say that Catholics use it to confirm that Jesus is truly God, and some early Protestants, including Luther, also accepted it.
church_of_the_east.theotokos:
The Church of the East, which includes the Assyrian Church of the East, has historically preferred to call Mary the Mother of Christ, in Greek Christotokos, rather than Theotokos, Mother of God. The reason was concern that the title Mother of God might suggest that the divine nature had a mother, and might confuse the two natures of Christ.

The church honors Mary highly, and in the Common Christological Declaration of 1994 with the Catholic Church, it explained that it uses the phrase Mother of Christ our God and Saviour, and recognizes that the Catholic use of Mother of God is a legitimate way of confessing the same faith. Other churches sometimes wrongly called this church Nestorian. A Protestant reader who knows the Council of Ephesus should note that this church stands on the other side of that dispute, but holds the same faith in Christ.
oriental_ortho.theotokos:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, including the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, honor Mary as the Theotokos, the God-bearer or Mother of God. They accepted the Council of Ephesus in 431, which affirmed the title, and they hold it as fundamental to their teaching that Christ is one person, fully God and fully man.

The title is used constantly in their hymns, liturgies and prayers, and Mary is honored with great devotion. It is understood as a statement about Christ more than a statement about Mary: because she bore the one who is God the Word made flesh, she is the Mother of God. A Protestant reader for whom the phrase Mother of God is unfamiliar should note that these churches use it to safeguard the truth that Jesus is God incarnate.
ortho.theotokos:
The Eastern Orthodox Church honors Mary as the Theotokos, a Greek title meaning God-bearer, or Mother of God. It was affirmed by the Council of Ephesus in 431 in order to protect the truth that Jesus is one person, both God and man, so that the one whom Mary bore was God incarnate.

The title is central to Orthodox worship. It appears constantly in hymns and prayers, and icons of the Theotokos holding the child Christ are found in every church. The Orthodox stress that it is a statement about Christ, and not a claim that Mary is the origin of God. A Protestant reader who uses the phrase mother of Jesus should note that the Orthodox regard Theotokos as an essential confession of the Incarnation, which most early Protestants also accepted.
adventist.tithing:
Adventists teach that the tithe, a tenth of one's income, belongs to the Lord, and that it is to be returned to the church as an act of faithfulness. They base this on the Old Testament, including the book of Malachi, and on Jesus' affirmation of tithing, and they regard it as a continuing responsibility of Christians.

Tithe is distinguished from offerings, which are given in addition, and it is used mainly to support the church's ministers and its mission. Adventist practice is that members return their tithe through their local church to the wider church organization, and it is treated as sacred. Many Protestant churches encourage giving, using the language of stewardship, and some teach tithing, but do not always make it as central. A Protestant reader should note that for Adventists tithing is a widely practiced and clearly defined part of church membership.
catholic.tithing:
Catholics do not have a fixed rule of tithing, or giving a tenth of income. The Church teaches that believers have a duty to provide for the needs of the Church, according to their means, which is one of the precepts of the Church, and it speaks of this as stewardship: the responsible use of all that God has given.

Catholics give through the collection at Mass, through offerings to their parish and diocese and through special appeals and charities. Some Catholics choose to tithe, and in some countries, such as Germany, a church tax is collected by the state. The amount is left to conscience, with an emphasis on generosity toward the Church and the poor. A Protestant reader from a church that teaches tithing should note that Catholics stress generosity in proportion to one's means, without setting a percentage.
evangelical.tithing:
Many Evangelical churches teach tithing: that Christians should give a tenth of their income to the local church, drawing on the book of Malachi and on the practice of the Old Testament. Giving beyond the tithe is called an offering.

Evangelicals differ on how the principle applies. Some hold that the tithe is a binding standard for all believers, while others hold that it is a helpful starting point for generosity, and that under the New Testament giving should be cheerful and generous, and according to one's ability. Giving is presented as a response to God's grace, not a way of earning it. A Protestant reader should note that in many Evangelical churches tithing is preached regularly, and members may be asked to make commitments of giving, although it is generally not a condition of membership.
lds.tithing:
Latter-day Saints pay tithing, which means giving one tenth of their income to the church. They regard it as a commandment of God, and as an expression of faith, and many members meet with their bishop at the end of the year to declare their tithing.

The funds are used for the church's work, including building temples and meetinghouses, supporting missionary work, education and administration. The church has no paid local clergy, so tithing does not pay pastors. Paying a full tithe is required for a member to receive a temple recommend. Members also give a separate fast offering to help the poor. A Protestant reader from a church that leaves giving to conscience should note that Latter-day Saints regard tithing as a clear standard, connected with promised blessings.
catholic.tongues:
Catholics recognize the gift of tongues as one of the charisms described in the First Letter to the Corinthians, and in the account of Pentecost in the Acts of the Apostles. Some Catholics, especially those involved in the Catholic Charismatic Renewal, pray in tongues, both privately and in prayer meetings.

The Church does not teach that speaking in tongues is required of Christians, or that it is a necessary sign of the Holy Spirit. Its pastors are responsible for discerning charisms, for ensuring that they are used in an orderly way and that they build up the Church. Tongues are rarely used in ordinary parish worship. A Protestant reader from a Pentecostal tradition should note that Catholics regard tongues as a legitimate gift but not as the evidence of Spirit baptism, and that it is a small part of Catholic life.
oneness_pentecostal.tongues:
Oneness Pentecostals speak in tongues, and most teach that this is the initial evidence of receiving the Holy Ghost. Following the accounts in Acts, they expect that a person who is filled with the Spirit will speak in a language given by the Spirit, which the speaker has not learned.

Tongues are also used as a prayer language and, with interpretation, as a gift in the assembly. Oneness teaching treats tongues as an expected sign that the Holy Ghost has come and as a mark of the new birth. A Protestant reader from another Pentecostal church should note that many Pentecostals also expect tongues, but generally regard Spirit baptism as an experience separate from salvation, while Oneness Pentecostals include it as part of the new birth.
pentecostal.tongues:
Pentecostals speak in tongues, also called glossolalia: speaking words that the speaker has not learned, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit. In personal prayer it is understood as a spiritual language for praise and intercession. In the congregation, a message in tongues is to be followed by an interpretation, so that the church is built up.

Many Pentecostal denominations teach that speaking in tongues is the initial physical evidence of baptism in the Holy Spirit, drawing on the accounts in Acts. Not every Pentecostal body holds it in the same way. Pentecostals do not regard it as a requirement for salvation, and they teach that the gift, like the others, must be used in order and in love. A Protestant reader from a tradition that does not practice tongues should note that Pentecostals treat it as a normal part of Christian experience and worship.
reformed.tongues:
Historically, Reformed churches have taught that the miraculous gift of tongues in the New Testament was a real speaking of known languages, as at Pentecost, and that it served as a sign to confirm the apostles' message in the early days of the church. Many Reformed Christians teach that this gift has ceased.

They also stress the apostle Paul's instructions for order in worship, where what is spoken must be understood and the church built up. Today there are Reformed Christians who are open to the gifts, but the historic and still most common view is that tongues, like other apostolic sign gifts, was given for a particular period. A Protestant reader from a Pentecostal or charismatic church should note that the Reformed emphasis falls on the completeness of Scripture and on the church's strength in preaching and love, and not on such signs.
catholic.total_depravity:
Catholics do not teach total depravity, the view that human nature has been so corrupted by sin that people are wholly incapable of any good. They teach instead that human nature is wounded by original sin, but not destroyed. Reason and free will remain, and human beings can know God to some degree and do things that are good in themselves.

The wound shows itself in ignorance, weakness of will, suffering and an inclination to sin called concupiscence. The Council of Trent taught that free will was weakened but not lost. Yet Catholics also teach that no one can be saved without grace, and that human beings cannot reach their supernatural end alone. A Protestant reader from the Reformed tradition should note that Catholics speak of a wound that grace heals, and not a complete inability, and that they use the image of illness rather than death.
ortho.total_depravity:
The Eastern Orthodox Church does not teach total depravity. It holds that the Fall corrupted human nature, bringing death, weakness and a tendency to sin, but it did not destroy the image of God in human beings, or their capacity to respond to God. Human beings remain free, and are able to cooperate with God's grace.

The Orthodox distinguish this from the Reformed idea of total inability, which they regard as too pessimistic, and as depending on the idea of inherited guilt, which they do not accept. Salvation is understood as healing of a damaged nature and as growth in union with God, in which God takes the initiative and the person freely responds. A Protestant reader from the Reformed tradition should note that the Orthodox agree that human beings cannot save themselves, but hold that they are not wholly corrupt.
reformed.total_depravity:
Reformed churches teach total depravity, sometimes called total inability. It does not mean that every person is as evil as possible. It means that sin has affected every part of a person, including the mind, will and affections, so that no one can save himself or even truly desire God without God's grace.

Reformed Christians also affirm that unbelievers can do good in a civil and social sense, because of common grace, which restrains sin and gives gifts to all people. What they cannot do, by their own strength, is to please God in the sense of loving him above all and trusting Christ. The doctrine is intended to show that salvation must be entirely God's work. A Protestant reader from a Wesleyan or Arminian tradition should note that they also teach that people need grace, but hold that God's prevenient grace restores an ability to respond.
anglican.tradition:
Anglicans value the tradition of the church as a faithful guide to Scripture, especially the creeds, the worship of the early church and the teaching of the Fathers. They understand their church as both catholic and reformed: part of the ancient church of the West, and shaped by the Reformation.

The Book of Common Prayer is one of the main carriers of this tradition. Tradition is respected but is judged by Scripture, so that a custom which contradicts the Bible can be reformed. Anglicans differ about how much weight tradition should carry. Anglo-Catholics look to it more fully, and Evangelical Anglicans treat it more cautiously, but both take part in the same church. A Protestant reader from a church that gives little weight to tradition should note that Anglicans treat it as a real, though subordinate, source of guidance.
catholic.tradition:
Catholics use the word Tradition, with a capital letter, for the apostolic teaching which was handed down from the apostles in the Church, alongside Scripture. It includes the creeds, the liturgy, the practice of the sacraments and the teaching of the Fathers, and it is understood as a living transmission, guided by the Holy Spirit.

The Catholic Church teaches that Scripture and Tradition together form one deposit of the word of God, and that they are to be honored equally. Catholics distinguish Sacred Tradition from merely human traditions, which can change or be set aside. A Protestant reader who has in mind Jesus' criticism of the traditions of men should note that Catholics point to other passages, such as the apostle Paul's instruction to hold to the traditions received, and that they think of Tradition as the apostolic faith itself.
oriental_ortho.tradition:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, which include the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, honor Holy Tradition as the faith handed down from the apostles, and preserved in the life of the church. It includes the Scriptures, the creeds, the first three ecumenical councils, the writings of the Fathers, the liturgy and the canons.

They especially value the teaching of Fathers such as Athanasius and Cyril of Alexandria, and the traditions of their own churches, some of which go back to the earliest centuries. Tradition is not seen as separate from Scripture, but as the living context in which it is rightly understood. A Protestant reader who values Scripture alone should note that these churches regard Tradition as the way in which the Holy Spirit has kept the faith alive, and consider that the Bible cannot be separated from it.
ortho.tradition:
The Eastern Orthodox Church speaks of Holy Tradition as the life of the Holy Spirit in the Church, through which the faith of the apostles is handed on. It includes Scripture, which is its highest written form, and also the creeds, the decisions of the ecumenical councils, the writings of the Fathers, the liturgy, the canons and the icons.

The Orthodox do not regard Tradition as a fixed set of customs or as a second source alongside Scripture. It is the way in which the Church lives and understands the truth she has received. It is expected to be faithful to the past, and yet it is alive. A Protestant reader who contrasts Scripture with tradition should note that the Orthodox think of the Bible as belonging within Tradition, and consider that the church which produced and preserved the Bible is the proper context for reading it.
catholic.trinity:
Catholics confess one God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The three persons are distinct, and yet are one in being, sharing one divine nature, and equal in power, glory and eternity. This is the central mystery of the Christian faith, revealed in Scripture, and defined by the early councils, especially Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381.

The Church teaches that the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Trinity is professed in the Creed, in the sign of the cross and in the words of Baptism. A Protestant reader will find that Catholics and most Protestants share the same doctrine of the Trinity, and that the differences involve the procession of the Spirit and the way the doctrine is expressed in worship and prayer.
christadelphian.trinity:
Christadelphians hold that God is one, and that this one God is the Father. Jesus is the Son of God, born of Mary through a miracle of God's power, and is truly the Lord and Savior, but he is not himself God. The Holy Spirit is understood as the power of God, by which he acts and inspires, and not a separate person of the Godhead.

For Christadelphians this is simply what the Bible says, and they regard the Trinity as a later doctrine developed through Greek philosophy. Their use of the phrase God is one is meant to keep faith close to the wording of Scripture. A Protestant reader who confesses the Trinity should note that Christadelphians reject it, and see this as one of the main differences between themselves and the larger churches.
iglesia_ni_cristo.trinity:
Members of the Iglesia ni Cristo confess one God, the Father alone. Jesus Christ is honored as Lord, Savior and the one mediator between God and humanity, but is taught to be a man chosen and sent by God, not God himself. The Holy Spirit is understood as the power or work of God and not as a separate person.

Members hold that the doctrine of the Trinity is not taught in the Bible and entered Christianity after the apostolic age. They ground their own teaching in biblical passages that speak of the Father as the only true God. A Protestant reader who confesses the Trinity should note that most other Christian traditions disagree with this account of Jesus and the Spirit, and members are aware of that, but they present their teaching as a return to what Scripture says plainly.
jehovahs_witnesses.trinity:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that there is one God, Jehovah, the Almighty, who alone is the Creator. Jesus Christ is God's Son, whom they honor as Savior and King, but he is a separate and subordinate being, not equal to the Father. The holy spirit is God's active force, the power he uses to accomplish his will, and not a person.

For this reason Witnesses do not accept the doctrine of the Trinity. They point out that the word does not appear in the Bible and hold that the doctrine developed in later centuries, under the influence of ideas from outside Scripture. They cite Jesus' own words that the Father is greater than he is. A Protestant reader who confesses the Trinity should note that Witnesses know this is a point on which they differ from most Christians, and they aim to show from the Bible why they read the evidence differently.
lds.trinity:
Latter-day Saints believe in the Godhead, which consists of God the Father, his Son Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost. They teach that these are three distinct beings who are one in purpose, in love and in the work of salvation. The Father and the Son have glorified bodies of flesh and bone, and the Holy Ghost is a personage of spirit.

They do not accept the traditional doctrine of the Trinity, in which three persons share one being, since they hold that the three are separate. They understand passages that speak of their oneness as referring to unity of will and purpose, and not of substance. A Protestant reader who confesses one God in three persons should note that Latter-day Saints use the same names, and honor Jesus as God's Son and Savior, but describe the relationship among the three differently.
oneness_pentecostal.trinity:
Oneness Pentecostals teach the oneness of God: there is one God, not three persons, and this one God has revealed himself in different ways. Father, Son and Holy Spirit are understood as titles or manifestations of the one God, as he has acted in creation, in redemption and in the believer's life. They therefore do not accept the traditional doctrine of the Trinity.

Their teaching is based on passages such as the declaration that the Lord our God is one, and on the New Testament's identification of Jesus with God. Oneness Pentecostals believe that all the fullness of the Godhead dwells in Jesus. A Protestant reader who confesses the Trinity should note that Oneness Pentecostals affirm that Jesus is God and worship him as such, but do not speak of three persons in one God, and prefer words like manifestation or role.
oriental_ortho.trinity:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, which include the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, confess one God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who share one divine nature. They accept the Nicene Creed, and the teaching of the first councils on the Trinity, and use the same faith in their worship.

The Trinity is praised in their liturgies, in which the Trinitarian formula appears constantly, and in their hymns. They confess the Holy Spirit as proceeding from the Father, without the Western addition of and the Son. A Protestant reader will find that these churches share the classical doctrine of the Trinity with most Protestants, and should note that their dispute with other churches concerns the nature of Christ and the words used to describe it, and not the Trinity.
ortho.trinity:
The Eastern Orthodox Church confesses one God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who share one divine essence and are eternally united in love. The Orthodox emphasize that the Father is the source of the other two, with the Son eternally begotten of him and the Spirit eternally proceeding from him. The Greek word for person here is hypostasis, and the technical term for the Trinity is tri-hypostatic God.

The doctrine was defined at the early ecumenical councils and articulated by teachers such as the Cappadocian Fathers. The Orthodox think of the Trinity not only as a doctrine but as the model of communion which the church is called to reflect. The best-known icon of the Trinity shows three angels who visited Abraham, painted by Andrei Rublev. A Protestant reader will find that Orthodox and Protestants confess the same Trinitarian faith, with a difference over the procession of the Spirit.
unitarian.trinity:
Unitarian Christians hold to the unity of God: God is one, and that one God is the Father. Jesus is honored by many as the Messiah, a teacher and an example to follow, but is not held to be a second person within the Godhead. Unitarian Christians commonly say that the doctrine of the Trinity is not stated in so many words in Scripture and took shape later, and that the simpler confession of one God is the more faithful one.

There is real variety under this name. Some historic Unitarians saw Christ as a uniquely exalted human being, others as a created but pre-existent being. Many people who use the label today belong to communities that welcome people of several faiths. A Protestant reader who confesses the Trinity should note that Unitarian Christians read the same Bible and reach a different conclusion, giving weight to conscience, reason and the moral teaching of Jesus.
catholic.true_church_claim:
The Catholic Church teaches that the Church which Christ founded subsists in the Catholic Church, governed by the successor of Peter and the bishops in communion with him, and that it has the fullness of the means of salvation. This is the basis of its claim to be the one true Church.

The Church also teaches that many elements of truth and holiness exist in other Christian communities, that other baptized Christians are joined to it in some measure, and that people outside the visible Church can be saved, through no fault of their own. The old phrase that there is no salvation outside the Church is understood in this way. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics do not mean that other Christians are not Christians, but that the fullness of the Church is found in the Catholic Church.
iglesia_ni_cristo.true_church_claim:
Members of the Iglesia ni Cristo believe that their church is the true Church of Christ described in the New Testament, restored in 1914 in the Philippines through Felix Manalo, whom they regard as God's last messenger. They point to the name Church of Christ, which they read in the New Testament, and to biblical prophecies which they believe were fulfilled in the church's rise.

The church is led by an Executive Minister and has a structured process of doctrinal instruction before baptism and membership. Members see the claim as a matter of faithfulness to God's word, not of pride. A Protestant reader should note that other Christians generally do not accept this claim, and that members believe that joining the true church is a step of obedience.
lds.true_church_claim:
Latter-day Saints describe their church as the only true and living church on the face of the earth, using words from the Doctrine and Covenants. The same passage says that God is well pleased with the church collectively, and not individually, which Latter-day Saints take to mean that the statement concerns the church as an organization with priesthood authority and the fullness of the gospel, and does not judge individuals.

They believe that other churches teach much that is true and good, and that God works through many people. Members invite others to learn about the restored gospel through missionaries and personal example, and they hold that they have something to share, and not that others lack faith. A Protestant reader should note that the claim concerns divine authority and the completeness of teachings and ordinances, and that most other Christians find it exclusive.
ortho.true_church_claim:
The Eastern Orthodox Church holds that it is the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church founded by Christ and the apostles, and that it has kept the fullness of the faith and sacraments through history. It does not regard itself as one denomination among many, but as the continuation of the church of the New Testament.

Orthodox Christians are generally careful not to judge the standing of others before God. They say that they know where the Church is, but do not presume to say where it is not, and that God can save whomever he chooses. There are differences among the Orthodox on how far the sacraments of other churches are recognized. A Protestant reader should note that the claim is made in a spirit of responsibility for the faith, and not to disparage the faith of others.
restorationist.true_church_claim:
Many Restorationists say that they are not a denomination, but simply the New Testament church, and that they claim no name other than the biblical names for the church. For them this is a statement about faithfulness to Scripture more than a claim to superiority.

Restorationists do not agree among themselves on what this implies for other Christians. Some acknowledge that Christians exist in all churches, and hope for unity around the Bible. Others hold that only their own fellowship truly follows the New Testament pattern, and treat other churches as departing from it. A Protestant reader should note that most other Christians hear the claim as exclusive, and that Restorationists who make it usually say that it is meant as an invitation to return to the Bible together.
catholic.veneration:
Catholics distinguish between three kinds of honor. Latria, or adoration, is due to God alone. Dulia, or veneration, is the honor shown to the saints and angels. Hyperdulia, a higher form of veneration, is shown to the Virgin Mary alone, because of her unique place as the Mother of God.

Veneration is expressed by prayers asking for their intercession, by feast days, by images and relics, and by imitating their lives. The Church teaches that the honor passes to God, who works in them. Many Protestants call this the worship of saints and reject it as idolatry. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics insist that worship and veneration are different, and do not offer the saints the adoration that belongs to God, though they recognize that the distinction can be lost in practice.
ortho.veneration:
The Eastern Orthodox Church distinguishes between worship, which is due to God alone, and veneration, which is honor shown to the saints, the Mother of God, the cross, icons and relics. Veneration is expressed by bowing, making the sign of the cross, kissing an icon, lighting a candle, and burning incense before it.

The Greek word for the bow or prostration is proskynesis. The Seventh Ecumenical Council in 787 taught that the honor shown to an image passes to the person depicted. Orthodox Christians understand veneration as a way of honoring the friends of God, and, through them, God himself. A Protestant reader who calls this worship of saints should note that the Orthodox reject the charge, and hold that the same physical gestures can be given a different meaning, as a person may bow to a king or to God.
catholic.virgin_birth:
Catholics confess that Jesus was conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary, without a human father, and that Mary remained a virgin. This is affirmed in the Creed: he was conceived by the Holy Spirit, and born of the Virgin Mary. The Church teaches that it is a sign of Jesus' divine origin and of the new creation.

Catholics distinguish the virgin birth of Jesus from the Immaculate Conception, which concerns Mary's own conception, and from her perpetual virginity, which concerns her whole life. A Protestant reader will find that Catholics and most Protestants share belief in the virginal conception of Jesus, and should note that Catholics see it as connected with other teachings about Mary that Protestants do not accept.
lds.virgin_birth:
Latter-day Saints affirm that Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary, who conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost. They accept the accounts in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, and the Book of Mormon also speaks of Mary as a virgin who would bear the Son of God.

They teach that God the Father is the literal father of Jesus' physical body, and Mary the mother, and that this gave Jesus both divine and mortal inheritance. The church has not defined the details of how this took place. A Protestant reader will find that Latter-day Saints share the belief in the virgin birth, and should note that their teaching about God's fatherhood of Jesus' body differs from the more common view that the conception was a miraculous act of the Holy Spirit.
ortho.virgin_birth:
The Eastern Orthodox Church confesses that Jesus Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, as the Creed says. It celebrates the announcement of the angel Gabriel to Mary, called the Annunciation, on March 25, as one of the great feasts of the church year.

The Orthodox teach that Mary remained a virgin throughout her life, and honor her as ever-virgin and Theotokos. The virgin birth is understood as a sign that the Incarnation is an act of God, and as the beginning of the new creation. A Protestant reader will find that Orthodox and Protestants share the belief in the virginal conception of Jesus, and should note that in Orthodoxy it is celebrated in worship, and is linked to the honor given to Mary.
catholic.visible_and_invisible_church:
Catholics teach that the Church is a single reality that is both visible and spiritual. It is a visible society with a structure of pope, bishops and priests, with sacraments and a teaching office, and it is also the mystical Body of Christ and the community of faith, hope and charity.

Catholics do not accept the idea of an invisible church, in the sense of a true church of the elect that is distinct from the visible institution. They hold that the visible Church includes both saints and sinners, and that Christ established it as a visible community. A Protestant reader who distinguishes the invisible church of all true believers from the visible church of all who profess should note that Catholics do not divide them, and see the Church as one visible communion that is also a divine mystery.
ortho.visible_and_invisible_church:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that the Church is one, and that it is both visible and mystical. It is visible in its bishops, its worship and sacraments, and its communities, and it is also the Body of Christ, in which earth is joined with heaven, and the living with the departed saints.

The Orthodox do not separate these into two churches, as in the Protestant distinction between the visible and the invisible church. The Divine Liturgy is understood as the place where the two are united, since the church on earth worships together with the angels and saints. The boundaries of the Church are not defined in legal terms, and God alone knows who belongs to him. A Protestant reader should note that the Orthodox stress that the Church is a visible communion and also a mystery.
reformed.visible_and_invisible_church:
Reformed churches distinguish between the invisible church and the visible church. The invisible church is the whole number of the elect, gathered from every age and place, known fully only to God. The visible church consists of all those throughout the world who profess the true religion, together with their children, organized in local congregations.

Both are real, and both are the church of Christ. The visible church is mixed, and contains some who are not truly believers, as Jesus' parable of the wheat and the weeds describes. It is marked by the preaching of the Word, the right administration of the sacraments and, in many Reformed statements, by discipline. A Protestant reader will find this distinction familiar, since it has been widely taken up in Protestant thought, and should note that Reformed churches make it a formal part of their teaching.
